title: Trapping Rain Water

concept.title: Water level = the lower of the two tallest walls around
body: On top of position `i` the water can rise up to `min(tallest wall to the left, tallest wall to the right)`, as long as that is higher than the bar itself. So the water above bar `i` is `min(maxLeft, maxRight) - h[i]`. Computing both maxima for every `i` would need two helper arrays.

Two pointers avoid them. Keep `l` and `r` at both ends and the largest bars `leftMax` and `rightMax` seen so far from each side. If `h[l] < h[r]`, the right side certainly has a wall at least as tall as `h[l]`, so the water at `l` depends only on `leftMax`: add `leftMax - h[l]` and move `l`. Otherwise do the same on the right.

statement: An elevation map is made of `n` bars of width 1 with the given heights. After rain, water is trapped between the bars. Print the total amount of water (the number of unit squares of water) that stays on the map. Water running over the left or right end is lost.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` heights.
outputFormat: Print the amount of trapped water.

examples.note: The trapped water amounts to 6 units.

hints: The water above a bar is the lower of the tallest bar on its left and the tallest bar on its right, minus the bar itself.
You can compute this with two helper arrays of prefix and suffix maxima.
Or use two pointers: process the side with the smaller current bar, keeping its running maximum.

explanation: The side with the lower end bar is the side whose water level is already decided by its own running maximum. Two pointers close in from the ends and add the water over each bar once.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
h = list(map(int, input().split()))

l, rr = 0, n - 1
leftMax = rightMax = 0
water = 0
while l < rr:
    if h[l] < h[rr]:
        leftMax = max(leftMax, h[l])
        water += leftMax - h[l]
        l += 1
    else:
        rightMax = max(rightMax, h[rr])
        water += rightMax - h[rr]
        rr -= 1
print(water)
